newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Jan 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business press - Jan 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- GOLDSMITHS PROFITS

High sales of diamond rings, earrings and branded watches in the four weeks to Christmas gave Goldsmiths jewellery group a like-for-like rise of 9.8 per cent. Chairman Piasecki said that customers appeared to compare prices in other shops much less this year, adding that Goldsmiths have no real competition on the high street. Goldsmiths makes almost 25 per cent of its annual sales in December, with turnover for the 11 months to December rising by 10.5 per cent, or 9.4 per cent on a comparable store basis.
-- SIEBE BUY SATCHWELL

Temperature controls group Siebe have bought Satchwell Controls from GEC for 80 million pounds stg, continuing expansion after buying Unitech for 520 million pounds stg earlier this year. As the largest British manufacturer and installer of building automation systems for industrial and commercial facilities, Satchwell employ 1,026 staff with sales of 60.3 million pounds stg and operating profits of 4.9 million pounds stg last year. A Siebe spokesman said Satchwell's operating margins were expected to rise from 8.1 per cent, to over 10 per cent, lifting operating profits to 6 million pounds stg.
-- MOBILE PHONE RECOVERY

Subscriber connection figures released yesterday from Vodafone and Cellnet show that the slowdown in the growth of the mobile telephone market is over. Vodafone announced that the only period which beat 1995 growth rates is the last quarter of 1996, but it still fell short of the final quarter of 1994, in which 200,000 people net signed up. Cellnet lifted its subscriber base by 143,000 in the last quarter, to 2.68 million customers. Both companies are currently attempting to switch customers to the digital system.
THE TIMES
-- BIGGER MAC MEANS 5,000 JOBS TO BE FILLED IN 1997

Fast food restaurant chain McDonald's has announced plans to create 5,000 new jobs in Britain this year, most of them part-time. The US company is to invest over 116 million stg on 110 new outlets, most of them drive-thru's in out-of-town retail parks or multiplex cinemas. Last year McDonald's opened 90 new restaurants, creating almost 4,500 new jobs. McDonald's claimed 78 per cent of the UK burger market in the last three months of 1996, according to figures from Taylor Nelson.
-- COMPUTER SOFTWARE PIRATES LOG A BILL OF 287 MILLION STG

A survey commissioned by the Business Software Alliance and the Software Publishers Association has found that British software pirates are costing the industry over 287 million stg a year. The figures put Britain as the world's seventh worst offender for illegally copied computer programmes. Worldwide, the report estimates the cost of piracy in 1995 at 8.4 billion stg.
-- DISPUTE BAD FOR BUPA'S HEALTH

A dispute between British private healthcare group Bupa and the Irish government has harmed the company's operations in the Irish Republic, Bupa conceded on Thursday. The row, which centres on Bupa's insurance packages, escalated on Thursday when the Irish Minister of Health apparently threatened legal action against the British company if it doesn't change its schemes.
THE GUARDIAN
-- DIRECTORS ON DOUBLE WINNER

The Association of British Insurers (ABI) has accused company directors of hijacking recommendations designed to link executive earnings to performance. The ABI claims directors are using the recommendations, made by the Greenbury committee, which examined the issue of executive pay, to justify entirely new layers of boardroom pay. The ABI allegations were made in a submission to the Hempel Committee on corporate governance.
-- DEATH BY FRANCHISE FOR NATIONALISED JOKE

British Rail, the national railway operator which has been the butt of jokes - ranging from the quality of its catering to the inventiveness of its excuses for late or non-running trains - for the past 50 years, will move even closer to full privatisation this weekend when another four rail passenger franchises begin operation. Only seven of BR's 25 passenger franchises remain to be sold off.
-- OECD URGES JAPAN TO THINK SLIM

The OECD, the leading think-tank of the industrialised nation, has launched its latest survey of the Japanese economy by claiming that the country needs a diet of spending cuts and tax increases to tackle its bloated public sector deficit. The survey also recommends that over the longer term, continuing deregulation of Japan's overprotected consumer markets is the key to raising the growth rate.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- FORD SALES PLUMMET

According to internal minutes, Ford has threatened that the future of the company in the UK is at stake. Sliding market shares and anxiety about the Halewood plant on Merseyside are symptomatic of British Ford's 2.9 billion dollar US loss over the last seven years. Market share has dropped to below 20 per cent for the first time since a high of 26 per cent in the 1980s. European operations are also declining but personnel director, Bob Hill, emphasised that Britain was faring the worst.
-- TELEGRAPH PENSIONS FROZEN

The Telegraph Group has admitted that due to disappointing profits in 1996, it cannot meet increases to pensions payable to retired employees. The original pension plan had been non-contributable for employees, and in past years the firm has made "in-gratia" payments in a bid to keep the pensions in line with inflation. Jeremy Deedes, the managing director, blamed tough competition from The Times for the low profits, and told pensioners the matter would be reviewed in 1997.
-- GUARDIAN FLOTATION CANCELLED

Despite strong support from some board members, the Guardian Media Group has decided against flotation of non-core holdings. Proceeds of sales of stakes in Auto Trader and other publications were to support the core newspapers, the Guardian and the loss-making Observer. The decision, which has ended months of discussion, was taken as officials decided the non-core assets would be very useful to the group. BMC +44-171-377-1742
